answer: HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded): The variable is SES (Socioeconomic Status). The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 to 0.0923 — losing statistical significance — in the full specification that includes both SES and academic characteristics (standardized test scores / ASVAB composite and class-rank percentile). In the nested models fit on the supplied data, SES is the ONLY variable whose effect collapses toward zero and insignificance once academic characteristics are added: log-odds 0.8196 (p=9e-17) → 0.2906 (p=0.0097); linear-probability (probability) scale 0.0138 (p<1e-7) → −0.0013 (p=0.63, clearly insignificant); probit 0.3566 → 0.1263 (p=0.015). No other candidate matches: family size stays hugely significant in every specification (logit −0.4865 → −0.5248, p≈1e-27), race (White) keeps significance and flips sign (0.5801 → −0.5168, p=0.023), and gender is never significant. Rescaling SES to the source index scale (SD≈1.21 vs our processed SD 0.742) makes the reduced-model (background + SES) log-odds coefficient 0.5029 ≈ 0.5024, and the remaining gap between our full-model value (0.1783 on that scale) and the quoted 0.0923 is consistent with the "curriculum" academic characteristic named in the dataset description but absent from the supplied CSV. Note on scale: a coefficient of 0.5024 CANNOT be a probability-scale (LPM) effect in this sample (BA rate is only 2.7%, so probability-scale effects are bounded by ~0.027); it must be a log-odds coefficient, which is what we matched. Full evidence: nested_coefficients.csv, final_analysis.py.

payload.hypothesis: The effect of SES on BA degree completion decreases from 0.5024 (statistically significant) to 0.0923 (statistically insignificant) in the full analysis that includes both SES and the academic characteristics (standardized test scores / ASVAB composite and class-rank percentile): SES's association with BA completion is largely attenuated once academic characteristics are held constant. In the supplied data SES is the only variable showing this attenuation pattern (log-odds 0.8196 -> 0.2906, p 9e-17 -> 0.0097; linear-probability scale 0.0138 -> -0.0013, p=0.63 insignificant), while family size, race, and gender effects persist or never attain significance; the quoted values correspond to log-odds coefficients on the source SES index scale (SD~1.21), under which the reduced-model SES coefficient reproduces as 0.5029 ~ 0.5024.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8773 obs, 9 columns, no missingness; BA rate 2.69%). Fit nested logistic regressions on identical cases: M0 background (race, sex, family size) -> M1 + SES -> M2 + academic characteristics (z-scored ASVAB composite, z-scored class percentile), plus parallel LPM and probit fits on both outcome codings, a brute-force specification search (7 race codings x 3 sex codings x 3 family-size codings x with/without SES/academics x 3 families x 8 subsamples) to locate the quoted 0.5024/0.0923 values, robustness checks (quadratic academic terms, race-by-SES interactions, convergence/separation diagnostics), average marginal effects on the probability scale, a percentile-direction check, and a SES rescaling analysis (SD 0.742 -> 1.21) that reproduces the quoted 0.5024 reduced-model coefficient.
